Reserved
re-ZERVD
v. (past part.)
From Latin reservare, to keep back, to save up. Webster 1828: kept in store; retained; not delivered or given up. Peter uses it of an inheritance kept in heaven for believers, and of the unjust kept for the day of judgment — the same verb, two custodies.

Biblical Definition

Reserved is a word of custody, and Scripture uses it of two things being kept, one in hope and one in dread. Peter’s doxology gives the first: believers are begotten again unto a lively hope to an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away, reserved in heaven for you (1 Peter 1:4), and the next verse adds that they are kept by the power of God through faith — the inheritance is guarded for the heirs and the heirs are guarded for the inheritance. Nothing in that arrangement depends on the heir’s grip. The same apostle uses the word in the other direction: The Lord knoweth how to deliver the godly out of temptations, and to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment to be punished (2 Peter 2:9). Jude says it of the fallen angels: the angels which kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation, he hath reserved in everlasting chains under darkness unto the judgment of the great day (Jude 1:6). And there is a third and lovely use, in Elijah’s despair: the LORD answers that He has reserved seven thousand in Israel who have not bowed to Baal, which Paul takes up in Romans 11 as the doctrine of the remnant according to the election of grace.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines RESERVE as to keep in store for future or other use; to withhold from present use for another purpose; to retain; and RESERVED as kept for another purpose, retained, not given up. The custodial sense is exactly Peter’s.

expand to see more

RESERVE, v.t. — To keep in store for future or other use; to withhold from present use for another purpose.

To keep; to hold; to retain; as, to reserve a right or a portion.

RESERVED, pp. — Kept for another purpose; retained; not delivered or communicated.

RESERVED, a. — Restrained in words and actions; not free or frank — the modern conversational sense, absent from the Authorized Version.

From Latin re, back, and servare, to keep — the same verb behind preserve, conserve, and observe.

Key Scripture

1 Peter 1:4 — "To an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away, reserved in heaven for you,"

2 Peter 2:9 — "The Lord knoweth how to deliver the godly out of temptations, and to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment to be punished:"

Jude 1:6 — "And the angels which kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation, he hath reserved in everlasting chains under darkness unto the judgment of the great day."

Romans 11:4 — "But what saith the answer of God unto him? I have reserved to myself seven thousand men, who have not bowed the knee to the image of Baal."

Romans 11:5 — "Even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace."

Modern Corruption

1 Peter 1:4-5 is one of the strongest assurance texts in the New Testament, and it is weakened wherever the believer’s security is made to rest on the believer’s grip rather than on God’s keeping.

expand to see more

Peter states a double custody. The inheritance is reserved in heaven for you — out of reach of moth, rust, thief, and market — and the heirs are kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation ready to be revealed in the last time. The word rendered kept is a military term for a garrisoned city. Both halves are needed and neither is the believer’s own work: he does not guard the inheritance and he does not garrison himself. This is why the Reformed doctrine of perseverance is more properly called preservation. The saints persevere, truly and actively, because God preserves them, and the faith through which they are kept is itself His gift. An assurance grounded anywhere else fluctuates with the weather of the soul.

Romans 11:4 shows the same reserving at work in a discouraged prophet’s crisis. Elijah, under the juniper, told God he was the only one left. God’s answer corrects the arithmetic and the theology at once: I have reserved to myself seven thousand men — not there happen to be seven thousand, but I have reserved, and to myself. Paul then draws the conclusion for his own generation: there is a remnant according to the election of grace. A believer who concludes from the visible state of the church that God has lost has made Elijah’s mistake, and the answer is the same. God keeps His own count, and He is the one doing the reserving.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek tereo (G5083), to keep, guard, reserve, in 1 Peter 1:4, 2 Peter 2:9, and Jude 6; phroureo (G5432), to garrison, in 1 Peter 1:5; kataleipo (G2641) at Romans 11:4.

expand to see more

Greek tereo (G5083) — to watch over, guard, keep, reserve; used of both the inheritance and the unjust.

Greek phroureo (G5432) — to garrison, to guard as with a military post; kept by the power of God (1 Peter 1:5).

Greek kleronomia (G2817) — an inheritance; the thing reserved in heaven.

Greek kataleipo (G2641) — to leave over, to reserve; I have reserved to myself seven thousand men (Romans 11:4).

Greek leimma (G3005) — a remnant; the conclusion Paul draws at Romans 11:5.

Usage

"An inheritance… reserved in heaven for you (1 Peter 1:4) — the estate kept beyond the reach of loss."

"To reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment (2 Peter 2:9) — the same custody, the opposite outcome."

"I have reserved to myself seven thousand men (Romans 11:4) — God’s count against a prophet’s despair."
